response.sql: WITH cust_orders AS (SELECT c.customer_id, c.gender, COUNT(o.order_id) AS num_orders FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE c.gender IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(c.gender) <> '' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.gender), gender_totals AS (SELECT gender, SUM(num_orders) AS gender_orders FROM cust_orders GROUP BY gender), shares AS (SELECT co.customer_id, co.gender, co.num_orders, CAST(co.num_orders AS REAL) / gt.gender_orders AS share FROM cust_orders co JOIN gender_totals gt ON gt.gender = co.gender), avg_share AS (SELECT AVG(share) AS avg_share FROM shares) SELECT s.customer_id, s.gender, s.num_orders, s.share, s.share - a.avg_share AS gap_above_avg FROM shares s CROSS JOIN avg_share a WHERE s.share > a.avg_share ORDER BY gap_above_avg DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 10;

assumptions.assumption: Each customer's order count is the number of rows in Orders for that customer, and only customers with at least one order are included. A customer's share is their order count divided by the total order count of all qualifying customers with the same gender.
A customer has no gender recorded when gender is NULL or blank after trimming. Blank strings are treated as missing, which the request does not spell out.

The average share is the plain mean of every qualifying customer's share, pooled across genders, as the request says 'the average share across these customers'. A customer is above average when share is strictly greater than that mean, and the gap is share minus the mean.
